title: Worktrees: several branches checked out at once
objective: By the end of this lesson you can have two or more branches open simultaneously in separate directories, and you know when that is genuinely better than switching or stashing.

blocks.text: Switching branches replaces the files in front of you. That is usually fine — until you want to compare two versions side by side, run a long build on one branch while working on another, or hand a branch to a background process that must not be disturbed by your next switch.

A worktree gives you a second working directory attached to the same repository. Both are real checkouts, both share one history, and neither can be checked out on the other's branch at the same time.

blocks.caption: Creating and using one
lines: git worktree add ../project-review fix/upload-limit   # existing branch
git worktree add -b hotfix/urgent ../project-hotfix    # new branch
cd ../project-review     # a full checkout: build it, run it, edit it

blocks.title: One repository, several checkouts
blocks.text: The extra directories are not clones. They share .git, so a commit made in one is immediately visible from the other, and there is no second copy of the history to keep in sync. Disk cost is one working copy of the files, not another history.

rows: Comparing two versions in a running app
Both can run at once, on different ports
A long build or test run
It continues while you work on another branch
Nothing to stash; your work stays exactly as it is
Read and run it without disturbing your own checkout
Two agents or tasks working in parallel
Each gets its own directory and cannot overwrite the other's files

blocks.title: This is the setup that makes parallel AI-assisted work safe
blocks.text: When an assistant is editing files while you also edit them, a single checkout means both are writing to the same directory and each switch or revert affects the other. One worktree per task removes that entire class of collision: separate directories, separate branches, one shared history to merge from when each piece is done.

blocks.caption: Remove it when the task is finished
lines: git worktree prune                     # tidy records of directories deleted by hand
# forgot and deleted the folder manually? prune fixes the bookkeeping

blocks.title: Worktrees are temporary by design
blocks.text: Five stale worktrees mean five directories where you might edit the wrong copy, and five branches nobody has finished. Create one for a task, remove it when the task is done. If a worktree has lived for a week, it is a branch that needed a decision, not a directory that needed keeping.

items: The same branch cannot be checked out in two worktrees at once — Git refuses by default (--force can override it, at your own risk), which prevents two directories fighting over one branch
Use --detach to inspect a commit or tag in a worktree without occupying a branch
Files ignored by Git, such as local settings and installed dependencies, do not come with the new worktree — you may need to install them there
Stashes are shared across worktrees, so a stash pushed in one appears in the list of another

blocks.title: Run two branches at once
steps: Run: cd ../git-lab-experiment && echo 'experimental' > experiment.txt && git add . && git commit -m "Try something"
Run: cd ~/git-lab && ls          (your files are untouched)
Run: git log --oneline --all --graph -5   (the commit is visible — one shared history)
Run: git worktree remove ../git-lab-experiment && git worktree list
blocks.expected: Two directories on two branches at the same time, a commit made in one and immediately visible from the other, and a clean removal. Your original checkout never changed, which is the entire point.

cheatsheet: git worktree add <path> <branch> — check out another branch in a second directory
git worktree add -b <new-branch> <path> — create the branch at the same time
git worktree list — every checkout attached to this repository
Worktrees share one .git: a commit in one is instantly visible in the other
The same branch cannot be checked out twice by default; use --detach to inspect a commit or tag
Ignored files (local settings, dependencies) do not come along — install them again if needed
git worktree remove <path> when the task is finished; git worktree prune after manual deletion
One worktree per parallel task is what makes concurrent editing safe

checkpoint.prompt: What does git worktree add give you?

choices.A: A backup of the current branch
choices.B: A second clone with its own copy of the history
choices.C: A compressed archive of the working tree
choices.D: A second working directory for one repository

checkpoint.explanation: One repository, several checkouts. They share .git, so there is no second history to keep synchronised. Typically on a different branch — one repository, several checkouts.

checkpoint.prompt: You are mid-feature with uncommitted work when an urgent fix arrives. Why might a worktree beat stashing?

choices.A: Worktrees are faster to create than a stash
choices.B: Your current checkout stays exactly as it is

checkpoint.explanation: Nothing to stash, nothing to restore, and nothing to forget. The fix happens in a separate directory. Your half-finished state is never disturbed, so there is no restore step to get wrong later.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does Git refuse to check out the same branch in two worktrees?

choices.A: It would double the disk usage
choices.B: Two directories moving one branch pointer would clash
choices.C: It would corrupt the shared commit history for everyone

checkpoint.explanation: Use --detach to inspect the same commit instead. A branch is a single pointer. Two checkouts moving it independently is a contradiction, so Git prevents it up front. 'Clash' means two directories advancing one branch pointer would conflict.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is one worktree per task the safe setup for parallel work, including AI-assisted work?

choices.B: It hides the changes from other tools
choices.C: Each task gets its own directory and branch

checkpoint.explanation: Concurrent edits and branch switches cannot overwrite each other's files. The collision comes from two things writing into one checkout. Separate directories remove it; the shared history still lets you merge each piece when it is done.
